title: Langflow vs n8n Price and Limits for AI Workflows
summary: Langflow vs n8n differ in purpose: one builds AI applications, the other adds AI to workflows. Compare their cost and features to choose the right tool.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces fits in this decision


### A third option for agents that act across many apps


For teams whose agent has to act across many business apps, with a person approving before it does,[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing) , which MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run, gives the agent a library of integrations to act in. It's not a verdict between Langflow and n8n.


It's open source with an[MIT-licensed core](https://github.com/activepieces/activepieces/blob/main/LICENSE) and is self-hostable, and its AI agent step sits in the same flow as ordinary deterministic steps. The agent's reasoning and the actions around it therefore belong to one flow, not to two products joined by a webhook.


### Why one workflow means one log


That matters because of the problem this article keeps returning to. When AI logic lives in one tool and business steps in another, a failed run means opening two logs and matching them by timestamp.


In the Activepieces flow builder you can put an Agent step next to a plain step, such as "send this[Gmail](https://www.activepieces.com/pieces/gmail) message" or "append a row to[Google Sheets](https://www.activepieces.com/pieces/google-sheets) ", both of which are among the 741 integrations counted in its open source monorepo, which means you can probably automate most of your team's common tools.


The run trace for that flow records a single execution from the first step to the last. There is no second system and no callback to reconcile, so there is one place to look when something goes wrong.


### Checking the connector library


Where no connector exists, the agent can't act, so the connector library is the thing to check first.


Activepieces calls its connectors "pieces", and the[pieces library](https://www.activepieces.com/pieces) holds **741 integrations in the open source monorepo** , roughly 60% of them contributed by the community rather than written in-house, so the platform's catalog grows with user demand rather than being limited by the core team.


When we looked, the page read "Showing 502 integrations", sorted by popularity, with Webhook, Google Sheets, Gmail and HTTP at the top. That's a count of what exists, not of what is maintained well.


Look up the two or three apps your agent must write to and read how recently each integration was updated before trusting the headline number.


If a connector is missing, the same library still covers you. The HTTP integration sends requests and returns responses, so an app without a dedicated integration can still be reached through its API, at the cost of building and maintaining that call yourself.


### Approval steps, self-hosting and pricing to test


Treat the rest as questions to test, not assumptions. Confirm how the approval step pauses a run, what the self-hosted version leaves out compared with the cloud one, and how pricing counts a run that contains an agent.


If you want to test those against a real workflow, you can[try it free](https://cloud.activepieces.com/sign-up?ap_cta=blog_body&ref=%2Fblog%2Flangflow-vs-n8n-price-and-limits-for-ai-workflows) .


Activepieces is the better fit for teams whose agent must act across many business apps with a person approving before it does, judged on whether the agent and its surrounding automation live in one place.


Because the Agent step sits beside ordinary deterministic steps in the same flow, the run trace shows a single execution from start to finish, rather than two systems bridged by a webhook or callback.


Langflow and n8n each have their strengths, but if you want the agent's reasoning and its actions to be one flow and one log, Activepieces delivers that.
